principles: A session is a depreciating asset, not a fact you establish once. Validate it before every authenticated sweep (check_session_tokens validate), because an expired token turns every endpoint into a login wall and a scan will happily fingerprint that wall as the application.

Short-TTL bearers (OAuth access tokens are often 5 to 15 minutes) must be RE-CAPTURED proactively, not only when something fails. If the live browser tab stays logged in and the manual crawl is recording, the credential is being refreshed in the browser continuously; re-run the capture action to pull the current one.

Keep a SECOND account current at all times. Cross-account authorization testing (IDOR/BOLA) needs account A and account B both live in the same window; a dead B silently turns every id-swap into a 401 that reads as 'protected'.

BRIDGE THROUGH THE CORPUS, NEVER THROUGH THE BROWSER JAVASCRIPT. The Claude-in-Chrome extension redacts JWTs and sensitive values from javascript_tool results, so you cannot read a token out of the page and paste it in. The framework captures the full value server-side: get it with check_session_tokens capture_oauth or recapture, which read the recorded crawl, and read the stored value from the session_tokens row if you need it. This is a property of the extension, not the framework.

A 403 on the authenticated arm while an anonymous control gets 401 means the token was ACCEPTED and then denied authorization for that one resource (a feature gate or a foreign object). That is a LIVE session hitting an authorization boundary, not an expired one. Do not refresh on it.
not_honoured on a load-balanced target is frequently a missing routing cookie, not a dead credential. Look for a per-response backend header before touching the auth flow.

how_to_identify.note: Read the recorded login from the manual-crawl corpus (replay_request search_captures, or query manual_crawl_captures) and match these signals to pick the auth_type, then call this tool with it.
signals: A POST to an /oauth2/token or /token endpoint that returns access_token/id_token JSON -> oauth-oidc (and jwt-bearer transport).
Authorization: Bearer <JWT> on the API calls, with a short exp claim -> jwt-bearer / oauth-oidc.
A form POST of username+password that sets a session cookie and nothing else -> session-cookie (classic) or password.
A SAMLResponse form field or a POST to an ACS/assertion-consumer URL -> saml.
A login that only asks for an email, then a link clicked from email, no password -> magic-link.
A static key sent in a header like X-Api-Key or Authorization: Bearer <non-JWT opaque> that never changes between captures -> api-key.
A second factor prompt (6-digit code, push approval, SMS) after the password -> add the mfa overlay to whichever primary type applies.
A uniform 403/challenge page from every automated request regardless of a valid session -> fingerprint-bound (Cloudflare and similar).

entries.name: Username / password, no MFA
entries.transport: Usually a session cookie, sometimes a bearer minted from the credentials.
entries.ttl: Server session; often hours. Validate before each sweep rather than on a timer.
steps: Record the login sequence once as an auth flow (manage_auth_flows / the auth recording), so the framework can replay it.
check_session_tokens refresh replays that flow headlessly and stores the new token it issues.
check_session_tokens validate to confirm, before scanning.
gotchas: A refresh can report success without setting a value: the flow ran and minted nothing. Always validate after.
Replaying the full login in a loop can trip rate limiting or an account lockout.

entries.name: Username / password WITH MFA (TOTP, SMS, email OTP, push)
entries.transport: Session cookie or bearer, after a second-factor step.
entries.ttl: As the primary type; the MFA step only gates minting.
steps: check_session_tokens refresh starts the flow; at the MFA step it returns status needs_input with a run_id and an input_request.
Ask the operator for the code delivered out of band (never invent one). For a push 'approve' the input_request has no_value true, so it is just a Continue.
check_session_tokens provide_refresh_input with the run_id, step_id and value; it resumes and may complete or ask for the next value.
Validate after it completes.
gotchas: A TOTP code is valid for ~30s; ask for it just before answering.
SMS/email OTP can be rate limited; do not loop refreshes.

entries.name: Magic link / passwordless email
entries.transport: Session cookie or bearer set when the link lands.
steps: The link is delivered out of band and cannot be replayed headlessly. The operator (or the AI driving the browser) clicks it in the recording browser.
If a refresh flow is modelled with a magic-link step, it returns needs_input asking for the URL the link landed on; answer with provide_refresh_input value set to that URL.
Otherwise, after the browser is logged in and the crawl recorded it, check_session_tokens recapture reads the freshest session for the host from the corpus.
gotchas: Magic links are usually single-use and short-lived; capture immediately after clicking.

entries.name: OAuth2 / OIDC (hosted IdP: Cognito, Auth0, Okta, custom)
entries.transport: Bearer in Authorization on the API; the IdP session lives in cookies at the IdP.
entries.automatable: headless IF a refresh_token is present; otherwise re-capture from the recording browser
entries.ttl: Access token typically 5 to 15 minutes. Re-capture proactively.
steps: check_session_tokens capture_oauth scans the manual-crawl corpus for this target and promotes the freshest OAuth token-endpoint response into a credential (and the refresh token if one was captured).

If it reports has_refresh false (no refresh_token in the exchange, common when the IdP refreshes via its own cookies), there is NO headless renewal: keep the browser tab logged in with recording on and RE-RUN capture_oauth whenever the bearer is near expiry.
If a refresh_token was captured, the session can be renewed headlessly via the modelled refresh flow.
Validate after each capture. Note the token mint host can be out of scope while the bearer is still in-scope-usable; capturing and using it is fine, probing the mint host is not.
gotchas: The bearer is held in SPA memory, not localStorage, and the extension redacts it from JS; capture_oauth from the corpus is the only reliable bridge.
Measured on Alpaca: authx bearer ~15 min, no refresh_token in the exchange, Cognito renews via browser cookies.

entries.name: SAML single sign-on
entries.transport: App session cookie set after the IdP POSTs a signed assertion to the ACS.
entries.ttl: As the issued app session; the assertion itself is one-time.
steps: The assertion is minted by the IdP and is not replayable headlessly. Log in through the browser with recording on.
check_session_tokens recapture reads the freshest app session cookie for the host from the corpus.
Validate before scanning.
gotchas: Do not try to replay the SAMLResponse; it is signed and single-use.
The IdP is frequently a different, out-of-scope host.

entries.name: JWT bearer in Authorization (possibly with a refresh cookie)
entries.transport: Authorization: Bearer <JWT>, sometimes paired with an httpOnly refresh cookie.
entries.automatable: headless if a refresh endpoint/cookie is replayable; otherwise re-capture
entries.ttl: Read the exp claim. Short (minutes) means re-capture often.
steps: Decode the exp claim to learn the TTL (the framework profiles this).
If a refresh cookie + refresh endpoint exist and are in scope, model them so refresh can renew headlessly.
Otherwise capture_oauth/recapture from the recording browser, same as oauth-oidc.
Store the companion refresh cookie with manage_session_tokens so it rides with the bearer.
gotchas: A bearer with no refresh material and a short exp is a re-capture loop, not a one-time add.

entries.name: Classic server session cookie
steps: Record the login as an auth flow for headless refresh, or recapture from the browser.
Store every companion cookie the session needs with manage_session_tokens, or the scan sends half the jar.
Validate against a route that refuses anonymous callers.
gotchas: Missing a companion/routing cookie reads as not_honoured on a load-balanced target; attach all of them.

entries.name: Static API key / long-lived token
entries.transport: A fixed header (X-Api-Key, Authorization) that does not change.
steps: Add it once with manage_session_tokens and activate it. No refresh is needed.
Re-validate only if the owner rotates it.
gotchas: Do not grade a static key with the honoured/not-honoured comparison expecting it to expire; it will not.

entries.name: Fingerprint/IP-bound session (Cloudflare and similar)
entries.transport: A clearance cookie bound to the real browser's IP and TLS fingerprint.
entries.ttl: As the clearance; but it will not travel to an automated client at all.
steps: The clearance is bound to the browser's IP and TLS fingerprint, so no captured session an automated client replays will be honoured.
Drive the crafted requests in the real browser (Claude in Chrome, or domdig for DOM sinks) and use its network panel as the repeater.
recapture keeps the framework's copy current, but expect the framework's own egress to be challenged; the win here is manual testing through the browser.
gotchas: A target that blocks your automated egress blocks every other automated attacker too, so the easy scanner wins are gone and the bug is waiting for whoever tests by hand.
